code:
K = lambda a: lambda b: a
B = lambda f: lambda g: lambda x: f(g(x))

double  = lambda x: x * 2
add_one = lambda x: x + 1

double_then_add = B(add_one)(double)   # add 1 after doubling
add_then_double = B(double)(add_one)   # double after adding 1

print(double_then_add(5))  # (5*2)+1 = 11
print(add_then_double(5))  # (5+1)*2 = 12

# B is derivable: B = S (K S) K
S = lambda a: lambda b: lambda c: a(c)(b(c))
B_from_SK = S(K(S))(K)
print(B_from_SK(add_one)(double)(5))  # 11 -- same as B(add_one)(double)(5)
description: Define the Bluebird combinator B = lambda f: lambda g: lambda x: f(g(x)) and derive it from S and K.

steps.description: Define K, the composition combinator B = lambda f: lambda g: lambda x: f(g(x)), and the helper functions double and add_one.

steps.answer: B(add_one)(double)(5) runs double(5) first and then add_one to give 11, whereas B(double)(add_one)(5) runs add_one(5) first and then double to give 12.
steps.question: What do double_then_add(5) and add_then_double(5) evaluate to?

steps.description: Compose add_one and double in both orders with B and evaluate both on 5 to print 11 and 12.
Define S and construct B_from_SK = S(K(S))(K), verifying that B_from_SK(add_one)(double)(5) also evaluates to 11.
Trace B_from_SK(add_one)(double)(5) to see S(K(S))(K) perform the same function composition as B.

title: The Bluebird B for Function Composition
